articles.title: Chrome with your source colours (spec only)
articles.summary: For a chrome material on existing artwork, choose the exact Foundation Chrome and Use source paint (spec only). This skips the primary base paint pass; other paint effects still need checking, and dark paint can look dark under metallic reflections.
articles.what: Foundation Chrome ID f_chrome starts at M/R/CC 255/2/16; Satin Chrome ID f_satin_chrome starts at 250/45/40. These registered plain materials have constant base spec. Use source paint (spec only) keeps the primary material from adding paint; the same primary source-lock principle is not restricted to a Foundation label. Source mode is different from Use finish’s own color. The final composed paint can still be altered by patterns, additional bases, HSB and source/target choices; final spec values also depend on strengths, overlays and masks. A dark source can read as dark chrome because metallic response changes reflections and colour impression. Do not lighten protected artwork automatically just to chase a mirror look.
when: You want your finished livery to be shiny chrome without changing the colours.
You want satin or brushed metal over your paint.
how: Identify the artwork and zone/layer intended to receive the metallic material.
Choose exact Foundation Chrome f_chrome, or Satin Chrome f_satin_chrome when that starting response is wanted.
Set BASE COLOR to Use source paint (spec only).
Inspect additional-base paint, patterns and HSB if the colour preview changes.
Compare the result under actual in-sim lighting before deciding whether a different material or a deliberate paint change is needed.

faq.q: Is Use finish own colour the same as spec only?
faq.a: No. Use source paint skips the reviewed ordinary primary base paint function. Finish-colour mode permits that material’s paint function instead; a plain paint_none material may produce no extra palette in either mode.

faq.q: Will choosing Foundation Chrome protect every sponsor automatically?
faq.a: No whole-project guarantee follows from that choice. Use source paint skips the primary base paint pass, but patterns, additional bases, HSB and the target can still affect artwork.

faq.q: Why can chrome look dark even when the paint pixels were preserved?
faq.a: High metal changes reflected colour and brightness, so dark paint can read as dark chrome. Inspect the source colour and lighting before changing artwork; material-only preservation does not mean identical in-sim appearance.

faq.q: Are Foundation Chrome values guaranteed in every exported pixel?
faq.a: No. The registered constant start is 255/2/16, but strengths, other spec contributors, masks and composition can change final values.

faq.q: Does source paint turn off overlay colour?
faq.a: No. The reviewed source lock skips the primary base paint pass. Additional-base paint and paint patterns remain separate contributors and must be checked.

articles.title: Retro stripes and numbers
articles.summary: The fastest way is to type it in Chat: "retro red white and blue stripes, flat with chrome trim". By hand, build each stripe as a box zone with a solid colour and recolour the numbers that your template already has.
articles.what: Shokker is not a drawing program; it paints your template with materials. Stripes come from zones (a coloured area with a finish), from your template's own art, or from artwork you add as a layer. Numbers are not typed in either: they exist in the template or you add them as a picture.
when: You want a classic racing stripe look.
You want different colours or finishes on stripes and numbers.
how: Fast way: open CHAT and type the look (for example "retro red white and blue stripes, flat with chrome trim"). Refine with "thinner", "make the red orange", "matte". Undo any step.
By hand: for each stripe press + Add Zone, open APPLY AREA, press Draw box and drag a long rectangle along the hood, roof or side on the flat sheet.
Give the stripe zone a base (Gloss is a good start) and set BASE COLOR to Use solid color for the stripe colour. Repeat for the white and the blue.
Add the Pinstripe pattern (thin lengthwise pinstripes) or Chevron under PATTERN for extra detail, and set Paint mode to Blend so it keeps your stripe colour.

Numbers: if your template has a Numbers layer, press the zone icon on that layer and give it a finish, or recolour it with BASE COLOR set to Use solid color. To add new lettering, type it with the Text tool (press T) or place a transparent PNG with Actions > Place image... in the layer list and move it with Move (V).
Put the stripes above the body zone in the list so they win. Render and check the CAR view.

tips: Three colours in a 60-30-10 split look professional: one dominant colour, one accent, one trim.
Line the stripes up across the car: the side band continues the bumper colour.
pitfalls: Boxes work on the flat sheet, where hood, roof and sides are separate rectangles.
One side of the sheet may be upside down relative to the other.

when: You want a clean, professional two-colour scheme.
You are not sure how many zones to make.
how: Open the exact template and identify the two colour regions using actual artwork layers or checked masks. Decide where their boundary belongs on this car.
Add/edit a Zone for each intended treatment and restrict it to verified coverage. Shared RGB or a generic panel box does not guarantee spatial separation.
Choose each Zone’s colour and material separately. Use source paint for ordinary primary material-only changes, and inspect other bases/patterns if they also affect colour.

articles.title: Choosing a colour-bearing Chameleon look
articles.summary: A colour-bearing Chameleon finish generates its own palette. Protect printed artwork and inspect the resulting paint and spec; its name is not proof of camera-angle colour flipping.
articles.what: The reviewed Foundation Chameleon ID chameleon generates a static spatial interference-colour field and a varying spec map. Its source functions do not accept a live camera angle. Lighting and reflections may change the visible impression, but dynamic pigment colour-flipping is not guaranteed from the name or a still swatch. Other Chameleon catalog variants need their own source and in-sim checks. In the reviewed ordinary primary-base compositor, BASE COLOR Use source paint (spec only) skips the primary base paint function, including a colour-generating one. Use finish’s own color allows that palette to run. This preserves the source from the primary base paint pass, not from every other operation: patterns, additional bases, hue/saturation/brightness, explicit colour overrides and target/mask choices need separate checks. Spec still changes reflections and the visible impression.

faq.q: Does a Chameleon finish automatically flip hue when the camera moves?

faq.q: Can COLOR FLIP use camera angle instead of changing the saved paint RGB?
faq.a: The inspected Color Lab applies a dark-value-weighted YIQ hue rotation to RGB arrays using a degree setting. It has no live camera-angle input. That operation changes texture colour treatment; camera motion and lighting are separate from its source math.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: The Flip degree setting feeds a YIQ transform with value-dependent weighting and clipping. It does not guarantee neighbouring or opposite perceived hues at every pixel. Preview the actual RGB instead of promising a named hue relationship.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: Underglow screen-blends a warm gold-like or cool silver-like RGB field, selected from the mean chosen colour and weighted by source brightness. It does not reveal a separately simulated substrate, create under-car lighting or add emission.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: The inspected colour override chooses the Lab branch when base_color_depth is present; this condition is not a candy-ID whitelist. Whether a given path reaches that override still depends on composition, so do not promise every dial affects every finish.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: Depth zero removes the depth blend weight. Active Flip and Underglow are separate branches and can still change RGB. Check all three settings rather than calling depth zero a complete colour reset.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: Any active Lab-dial handler calls _spbEnsureColorLab. Absent depth becomes 0.65 and colour strength is pinned to 1; absent Flip and Underglow become zero. First touching a different dial can therefore activate the default depth treatment.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: Reset Color Depth calls the Lab initializer and sets depth to 0.65. It returns to the active default, not to an absent/off state. Use an appropriate prior-state Undo and inspect the other colour contributors when reversing the change.

deep.heading: Verified practical behaviour
deep.body: B COAT is an encoded material-control channel. The f_candy starting CC value is 16, but this is not a measured clearcoat thickness or a guarantee of the deepest appearance. Final composition and the simulator remain separate acceptance checks.

articles.title: Edit one thing without touching sponsors
articles.summary: To change the body while keeping numbers and sponsors, first inspect what the actual layers contain. Restrict the zone to a layer that holds only the artwork you intend to change. If protected artwork shares that layer, use a checked selection or mask, or separate the artwork first. Check the preview and rendered paint; a layer name alone does not guarantee preservation.
articles.what: A layer restriction limits the zone to the selected layer artwork. It protects numbers and sponsors only when they are outside that artwork and the selected coverage. Inspect the layer contribution rather than relying on names such as Car Paint or Body. If body paint and decals share a raster, use a checked mask or selection to exclude decals, or separate them before editing. Check the preview and rendered result against the original.
when: You want a new body colour but the same numbers.
A change painted over a logo.
how: Open a layered template and use the layer eyes to inspect what each layer contributes. Names such as Car Paint or Body are examples, not proof of the layer contents.
Select the body artwork you want to change. Add or edit its zone and restrict it to the verified artwork layer; leave number, sponsor and logo layers out of the restriction.

If numbers or sponsors share the same layer, restricting the zone to that layer also includes them. Use a checked selection or mask to exclude protected artwork, or separate it onto another layer before changing the paint.

On a flat TGA, colour picking can also select a same-coloured number or logo. Inspect the selected coverage and exclude protected areas before applying a change; the template labels do not establish panel or UV boundaries.

Apply the colour or finish, inspect the preview and RENDER result, and compare the numbers and sponsors with the original. Use Undo if the result changes artwork you meant to keep. Check the exported paint in iRacing.

controls.label: RESTRICT TO LAYERS
controls.effect: Aims a zone at one layer only.

controls.label: Decal Rescue Kit
controls.effect: Plain non-metal spec under stamped numbers and sponsors.

tips: Inspect a layer with its eye before selecting it; its name alone does not prove which pixels belong to it.
An unrestricted zone can affect numbers and logos within its coverage. Check the actual preview and rendered paint.
pitfalls: A layer may contain both body paint and protected artwork. A layer restriction alone cannot separate those pixels.
A flat paint may have body paint and numbers of the same colour; colour picking can select both.
aliases: change the car but keep logos

deep.heading: When layer restrictions protect decals
deep.body: A layer restriction limits the zone to the selected layer artwork. It protects numbers and sponsors only when they are outside that artwork and the selected coverage. Inspect the layer contribution rather than relying on names such as Car Paint or Body. If body paint and decals share a raster, use a checked mask or selection to exclude decals, or separate them before editing. Check the preview and rendered result against the original.

deep.heading: Flat paints and shared colours
deep.body: A flat TGA has no layer separation. Colour picking or a box can include numbers and logos, including artwork that shares the body colour. Inspect the selected coverage and exclude protected artwork before applying a finish. A box or colour name does not identify UV panels or prove preservation. Undo a result that alters artwork you meant to keep.

deep.heading: If numbers look wrong afterwards
deep.body: First compare the artwork with the original. If paint or artwork changed unexpectedly, use Undo or restore the original. Decal Rescue Kit offers decal material presets; it does not restore lost artwork or prove that a selection excluded the decals.

examples.title: Body only
examples.goal: Illustrative setup after checking that the named body layer contains only the intended body artwork.

settings.BASE / COLOR: The colour and finish you want

examples.result: If the selected layer is isolated body artwork and the zone coverage excludes the protected decals, this setup limits the finish to that artwork. Verify the preview and rendered result.

examples.title: Ask Chat

settings.Message: change the body but leave the numbers alone

examples.result: Tell the helper which artwork to change and which numbers or sponsors to preserve. Check its proposed scope and actual preview; a reply saying it kept them is not proof. If the scope cannot isolate the artwork, use a checked mask or separate layers first. Use Undo for an unwanted change.

faq.q: Which layer is the body?
faq.a: Names such as Car Paint or Body are hints. Use the layer eyes to inspect its contribution and check whether it also contains numbers or sponsors.

faq.q: What does Everything or Remaining touch?
faq.a: Inspect the zone coverage and its layer restriction. Unrestricted coverage can reach protected artwork; selecting only a layer still includes every selected pixel of that layer.

faq.q: Can Chat change the numbers?
faq.a: Ask explicitly for the number artwork and check the proposed target and preview. For a body-only change, state that the numbers and sponsors must be preserved; the helper still needs an isolated scope.

mistakes.symptom: Numbers got a whole-car finish
mistakes.cause: The zone coverage included the number artwork, through an unrestricted scope or a shared artwork layer.
mistakes.fix: Undo the unwanted change, inspect layer content and zone coverage, then restrict to isolated body artwork or exclude the numbers with a checked mask.

mistakes.symptom: Numbers sparkle behind metal
mistakes.cause: Decal material or spec under stamped numbers may need adjustment; confirm that the original paint artwork is intact.
mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered result. For a material issue, inspect Decal Rescue Kit presets; if the artwork itself changed, use Undo or restore it.

protips: Use layer names as hints, then inspect the actual layer artwork and selected coverage. A name does not prove isolated numbers, sponsors or exact edges. Colour picking can include same-coloured protected artwork; check the preview and rendered result.

articles.title: Gradient from roof to rocker
articles.summary: Give a zone BASE COLOR Custom gradient with two or more colour stops and a vertical direction, one zone per side of the car. Colour Scale and Colour Rotation zoom or rotate the gradient over the flat sheet.
articles.what: A gradient is painted across the whole 2048 square, not along the car. On the side panels the top of the sheet is the roof line and the bottom is the rocker, so a vertical gradient inside a box around a side panel fades roof to rocker. Several islands share the same columns, which is why one zone per side is the safe way.
when: You want a fade from the roof down to the rocker.

Repeat for the other side with its own zone. If that side of the sheet is upside down, reverse the stops or pick the other vertical direction.
Check the CAR view to confirm the fade follows the body, and use Color Scale and Color Rotation to zoom or rotate the gradient.

articles.title: Mirror one side to the other
articles.summary: Layer MIRROR reflects image coordinates; Mirror Mask changes Zone coverage. Neither calibrates opposite car panels. Inspect artwork orientation, actual target placement and separate material coverage before accepting the mirrored result.
articles.what: The layer mirror flips the image horizontally and reflects its bounding box across canvas width. This does not identify car doors or calibrate UV islands. Check the actual template and mapped car before accepting placement; do not promise universal opposite-side alignment. The actual region-mirror handler swaps values inside the selected Zone’s regionMask. It does not duplicate image layers or flip their pixels. Choose the operation for the thing being edited: Zone coverage versus Layer artwork. The handler reports No region to mirror when the selected zone or its regionMask is missing, and needs the paint canvas dimensions. A layer selected elsewhere is not a substitute for an actual Zone region mask. When the active horizontalMirrorDiffers history helper reports symmetry, the handler returns without pushing Undo. A no-op is not a new painted change. This guard depends on that helper being present; do not generalize it to every unrelated flip command. The region-mirror loop swaps columns only while x is below floor(width/2). The centre column of an odd-width mask remains in place. This is a mask-array rule, not a car-panel centreline or symmetry calibration. Correcting text orientation and positioning the image are separate decisions. A horizontal image flip does not discover the intended car panel. Inspect the copy’s bounding box and actual template placement rather than expecting a second flip or ROT90 to repair every UV mismatch. The mirror clone copies layer image/effects/adjustments and selects the new layer. Zone material coverage remains a separate system. Inspect the copied artwork and intended source-layer restrictions; a mirrored image is not proof that its counterpart received the desired finish.
when: You designed the left side and want the right to match.
Text or a logo is backwards on one side.
how: For artwork, select its actual layer and use the layer MIRROR control. It creates a horizontally mirrored copy and reflects its placement across the canvas width.
Check the copied text orientation and actual template islands; move/transform the copy where this template requires it. An image flip does not calibrate opposite car panels.
For Zone coverage instead, use Mirror Mask on an existing selected Zone region. It mirrors the coverage mask and does not copy or flip layer artwork.
Inspect the copy and the separate material coverage before accepting either result. A mirrored layer alone does not prove the intended material reached the opposite panel.

faq.q: Does Save as Template transfer my team scheme to another computer?
faq.a: The inspected Save as Template handler writes shokker_zone_templates into browser localStorage. This is local storage for that runtime profile/origin, not automatic account/cloud sharing. Exported recipes and full projects are separate workflows; do not promise this button shares artwork across machines.

faq.q: Does loading a Zone template preserve my exact painted masks and layer restrictions?
faq.a: The saved subset omits regionMask, spatialMask and modern layer restrictions. The load handler explicitly sets regionMask to null. A reusable settings list is not the original painted layout or proof of protected sponsor targeting. Re-establish and inspect masks/restrictions before applying it.

faq.q: Does Load Template append the team settings to the zones I already have?
faq.a: The inspected handler assigns zones=data.map(...), replacing the Zone list rather than appending it. It pushes Zone Undo first. Review the current work before loading and use the appropriate undo if needed; this is not an automatic merge or a full-project restore.

faq.q: Does the saved team Zone template include each driver Customer ID or the car artwork?
faq.a: The saved Zone fields do not include Customer ID, car-folder identity, image files or PSD pixels. Reused Zone settings are not a driver-specific exported paint or an exact car-template transfer. Check the correct target and export identity independently.

faq.q: Does a loaded team Zone template reproduce all my current Base and Spec settings?
faq.a: This handler serializes a specific legacy subset, including base/pattern/finish, intensity, scale and patternStack. It does not serialize every modern Base/Spec field. For example independent spec-scale settings and imported material-source data are absent from this subset. Check the current fields after loading instead of promising identical output.

faq.q: Does plain Wet Look generate wet streaks or glass panes automatically?
faq.a: No such artwork is promised. The wet_look registration uses paint_none with a material starting state and Perlin/noise flags; its final renderer/composition is not a water-streak or glass-pane generator.

faq.q: Are Cathedral Veil Smoked Glass and Glass Flake the same wet-glass finish?
faq.a: Current filtered identities are efx_cathedral_veil (Cathedral Veil), fo_smoked_glass (Shag: Smoked Glass) and efx_glass_flake (Glass Flake). They are three distinct constructions, not interchangeable aliases of Wet Look. Select exact IDs and inspect each paint/spec rather than treating the shelf wording as equivalence.

faq.q: Does choosing a glass finish guarantee window transparency stays correct?
faq.a: A glass-inspired material name does not establish window cutouts or diffuse-alpha preservation. Check the imported template, layer transparency and actual export path. A spec-map alpha is a separate material mask; it is not a replacement for paint/window transparency.

faq.q: Will resetting spec sliders always fix a dull wet-glass result?
faq.a: A reset does not diagnose every contributor. Check the exact base identity, source spec, strengths, overlay stack, material mask and freshness of the preview/output. Dull appearance alone is not evidence that a particular slider moved; preserve the desired paint and isolate one contribution before changing values.

faq.q: Does a dark G ROUGH preview by itself certify a glassy car finish?
faq.a: The G channel shows encoded roughness bytes, not a full lit rendering. Metallic, clearcoat, masking, paint brightness and final composition also matter. For wet_look R15 is a starting constant, not a universal appearance guarantee or proof that dark preview pixels belong to the intended panel.

articles.title: Weathered and aged paint
articles.summary: For a beat-up look, limit a wear recipe to one part: draw a box zone around the bumper, pick a worn finish (Sun Faded, Hardware: Battle Worn, Die-Back Patina), add a chip or orange-peel spec overlay and lower Base Strength so your paint shows.
articles.what: Weathering is a few fine layers: sun-faded paint, chips at the edges and a rough clearcoat. In Shokker that is a worn base finish for the look plus spec overlays for the shine damage. Fine detail matters, so keep the scale small.
when: You want a barn-find, battle-worn or desert racer look.
You want a fresh paint to look lived in.
how: Make a zone on the body (Car Paint only) or on the lower half with APPLY AREA > Draw box.
Under BASE pick Sun Faded (sun-bleached), Hardware: Battle Worn (worn through to metal at the edges), Die-Back Patina, or a rust or salvage finish.
Lower Base Strength (0 is your original paint, 100 is the full finish) to let your own colours show through the wear.
Open BASE > SPEC OVERLAYS and add Micro Chipping or Orange Peel Film for chipped and rough clear.
Recolour a worn finish that brings its own palette with Hue Shift (not a solid colour).
Render and check at 100 percent zoom: weathering should read as fine detail, not blotches.

articles.what: This is the checklist for a complete livery from a car's layered template. It strings together the articles in this section so you can run it as one routine, and it ends with the two steps people forget: template layers off and Ctrl+R.
when: You have a car's PSD template and want a finished, working livery.
You want a repeatable routine for every new car.
how: Open: Open Paint... > Layered template, choose the template. Wait for the layers to load.
Setup once per car: iRacing User ID (Customer ID), iRacing Car Folder (car menu), Custom Number or Sim-Stamped Number to match Hide Car Numbers.
Body: + Add Zone, tick Car Paint under RESTRICT TO LAYERS, BASE a finish and colour.
Accents: zones above the body for stripes, hood, roof, trim (Draw box or PICK COLOR FROM CAR), each with its own finish.
Numbers and sponsors: leave them alone, or give the Numbers layer its own zone (zone icon on the layer).
Switch OFF Wire, Mask, Car_Mandatory and the group named Turn Off Before Exporting TGA.
Check the preview and the R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT views; use Decal Rescue Kit if numbers look wrong under metal.
Press RENDER, wait for the Saved bar, Show my files to confirm, then Alt+Tab to iRacing and press Ctrl+R.

controls.label: RENDER
controls.effect: Builds and copies the paint and spec.

controls.label: RESTRICT TO LAYERS
controls.effect: Keeps the body zone off numbers and sponsors.

tips: Save a project as soon as the layout is right.
Save a template to reuse the layout on teammates' cars.
pitfalls: Forgetting the template layers off paints guide lines into the render.
A wrong ID or number mode gives no error in iRacing, just paint-shop colours.
aliases: why is iracing showing paint shop colours

deep.heading: The whole job as one routine
deep.body: Open the template and wait for the layers to load. Set the ID, car folder and number mode once per car. Make a body zone limited to Car Paint. Add accent zones above it. Leave numbers and sponsors alone, or give the Numbers layer its own zone. Switch OFF Wire, Mask, Car_Mandatory and the group named Turn Off Before Exporting TGA. Check the preview and the R METAL, G ROUGH and B COAT views. RENDER, then Show my files, then Alt+Tab and Ctrl+R in iRacing.

deep.heading: The two steps people forget
deep.body: Template layers off and Ctrl+R. Forgetting the layers paints guide lines into the render. A wrong ID or number mode gives no error in iRacing, just paint-shop colours.

deep.heading: Save while you are ahead
deep.body: Save a project as soon as the layout is right and save a template to reuse the layout on teammates' cars.

articles.title: A gradient from blue to gold to white
articles.summary: Put the gradient on the zone that owns the big body area: BASE COLOR, Custom gradient, then three colour stops and a direction. Remember the fade runs across the whole flat sheet, not along the car.
articles.what: A zone can fade between 2 to 10 colours. The fade is laid over the entire flat paint sheet in one direction, so left to right on the sheet is not always front to back on the car, and each side of the car sits in its own part of the sheet. If the zone only covers some colours of the paint, the gradient shows only there. For a fade that runs along the real car, so both sides match and the hood, roof and trunk carry on from each other, use Car > Car-Space Fade....
when: You want a fade from one colour through a second into a third, such as blue to gold to white.
You want a sunset, fade-out or ombre look on the body.
how: Pick or create the zone that owns the body area, and give it a coating finish such as Gloss, Pearl or Candy under BASE.
Set BASE COLOR to the custom gradient option.
Add three stops: deep blue at 0, gold at 50 and white at 100 (the stop positions run from 0 to 100).
Choose the direction that matches the flat layout: horizontal runs left to right across the sheet, vertical top to bottom, or one of the diagonal and radial options.
Look at the preview. If one side of the car fades the wrong way, give each side its own zone with its own gradient.

controls.label: Custom gradient
controls.effect: Colour stops fading across the zone in a chosen direction.

controls.label: BASE COLOR
controls.effect: Chooses where the finish gets its colour: your own paint, one solid colour, or a gradient.

tips: True colours help: deep blue, a warm gold such as #d4a017, and pure white.
Use a gradient for a deliberate whole-sheet effect. For a touch of colour coming into black, a coloured flake finish works better than a fade.
pitfalls: The fade does not line up from the side panel over the bumper or onto the other side. That is how a flat unwrapped sheet works, not a fault.
A finish that brings its own colour (chrome, carbon, holographic) ignores the gradient; use a coating base.
aliases: make a gradient from one colour to another

deep.heading: Setting it up
deep.body: A zone can fade between 2 to 10 colours. Pick the zone that owns the body area and give it a coating finish such as Gloss, Pearl or Candy. Set BASE COLOR to the custom gradient. Add three stops: deep blue at 0, gold at 50 and white at 100 (positions run from 0 to 100).

deep.heading: Direction
deep.body: Horizontal runs left to right across the sheet, vertical top to bottom, or one of the diagonal and radial options. Left to right on the sheet is not always front to back on the car.

deep.heading: Limits
deep.body: The fade does not line up from the side panel over the bumper or onto the other side; that is how a flat unwrapped sheet works. A finish that brings its own colour (chrome, carbon, holographic) ignores the gradient. If the zone only covers some colours of the paint, the gradient shows only there.

examples.result: A fade from blue through gold to white.

faq.q: How many stops can I have?
Why does one side fade the wrong way?
faq.a: Each side of the car sits in its own part of the sheet. Give each side its own zone.

faq.q: Why does chrome ignore it?
faq.a: Finishes with their own colour ignore gradients. Use a coating base.

mistakes.symptom: No gradient appears
mistakes.cause: A finish that brings its own colour
mistakes.fix: Use Gloss, Pearl or Candy.

mistakes.symptom: The fade breaks at the bumper
mistakes.cause: Unwrapped sheet
mistakes.fix: Use a zone per panel.

articles.title: Holographic candidates: paint colour versus material response
articles.summary: Use a current reachable holographic candidate and inspect its paint/material output; a retired function name is not a picker instruction.
articles.what: The current filtered picker includes Holo Flake and Holographic Drift in Foundation EFX, and Holographic Foil as another Base identity. They are distinct candidates. A holographic name alone does not establish diffuse rainbow paint, camera-driven hue rotation or a verified simulator appearance.
when: You want a prism or rainbow shimmer on a body, an accent or a whole car.
You want to keep your colour and add the shimmer on top.
how: Select the intended Zone and inspect its artwork coverage. Open BASE > Base Material and inspect the current Foundation EFX Holo Flake or Holographic Drift entries, or search Holographic Foil.
Compare the candidate's paint and separate metallic, roughness and clearcoat previews before selecting it. These names identify reachable candidates, not interchangeable or approved appearances.
Choose BASE COLOR deliberately and keep artwork/material targets separate. Source paint skips the ordinary primary paint contribution; other stack contributors still need checking.
Adjust generated detail and compare the actual car in the intended lighting. Do not infer automatic angle-driven rainbow paint from the title alone.
pitfalls: Source analysis and candidate selection are not native appearance approval.
A name, layer label or map colour is not calibrated geometry or a source-colour guarantee.
aliases: Does a holographic spec overlay contain a rainbow paint image
Does variation in R METAL prove holographic shimmer is visible on the car
Is holographic overlay strength 80 a verified ideal setting
Does a plain Foundation Pearl or Metallic base already generate a holographic texture
Can a material-only holographic recommendation guarantee the source paint stays unchanged through the whole render

deep.heading: Does a holographic spec overlay contain a rainbow paint image?
deep.body: The inspected holographic_flake material function returns a stacked M/R/CC field, not a diffuse RGB art layer. Combined map colours encode materials; they do not establish rainbow paint hues or wavelength-accurate holographic rendering. Choose a colour-art contributor separately when a visible RGB rainbow is required.

deep.heading: Does variation in R METAL prove holographic shimmer is visible on the car?
deep.body: R METAL is the red metallic channel view. Variation shows differing material bytes, not verified shimmer, legibility, spectral colour or a native-car result. Inspect the other channels and actual lit target before approving the look.

deep.heading: Is holographic overlay strength 80 a verified ideal setting?
deep.body: Eighty is a proposed starting value, not a measured optimum or native appearance acceptance. Mask, stack, existing material and actual lighting affect visibility. Compare a restrained and stronger treatment on the intended target instead of guaranteeing a quality result.

deep.heading: Does a plain Foundation Pearl or Metallic base already generate a holographic texture?
deep.body: The exact plain f_pearl and f_metallic Foundation identities are pinned to constant material fields and paint_none. They do not add patterned hologram construction by themselves. A separate textured/colour-bearing contributor is a different choice; similarly named cards are not interchangeable.

deep.heading: Can a material-only holographic recommendation guarantee the source paint stays unchanged through the whole render?
deep.body: A spec contribution is distinct from the full composition. Ordinary primary Source mode skips that base paint function, while extra bases, patterns and colour treatments can still modify RGB. Inspect the complete composed paint before promising exact livery preservation.

articles.title: Matching accents on the rear of each side
articles.summary: Make a zone that takes the accent colour but only on the rear part of the sides, then give it the chrome-flake look. Read the real accent colour from the front first rather than guessing a blue.
articles.what: The front and rear accents share a colour, so a normal colour pick would catch both. You limit the new zone to the rear with a box or a named part, and put it above the zone that already owns the accent so it wins that area.
when: The livery has accent stripes front and rear and only the rear ones should change.
You want a metal-flake look on part of a shape that has the same colour elsewhere.
how: Pick the accent colour with PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the front accent so the zone matches it exactly.
Under APPLY AREA, use Draw box around the rear of the left side. Repeat on the right side, or use a car part if the car is known.
Choose a chrome or metallic finish under BASE, and keep the BASE COLOR on your own paint or the same blue.
Add a flake spec overlay with + ADD SPEC OVERLAY, with Strength about 70.
Move the zone to the top of the list, because the top zone wins overlaps, and check the preview.

controls.label: PICK COLOR FROM CAR
controls.effect: Takes the exact accent colour from the paint.

controls.label: Draw box
controls.effect: Limits the zone to the rear area.

tips: Never guess "the same blue". Sample the accent that is already on the car.
Chat can do this too: name the part and the look, then check the preview.
pitfalls: If the new zone sits below the zone that owns the accent colour, it will not show. Drag it up.

deep.heading: The idea
deep.body: Front and rear accents share a colour, so a normal colour pick catches both. Limit a new zone to the rear with a box or a named part and put it above the zone that already owns the accent so it wins that area.

deep.heading: Sample, do not guess
deep.body: Pick the accent colour with PICK COLOR FROM CAR on the front accent so the zone matches exactly. Never guess "the same blue".

deep.heading: The look
deep.body: A chrome or metallic finish with BASE COLOR on your own paint, plus a flake spec overlay at Strength about 70.

settings.APPLY AREA: Draw box around the rear of the left side, repeat on the right

examples.result: The rear accents glitter and match the front colour.

examples.title: Using a named part

settings.Choose: A car part if the car is known

examples.result: The zone lands exactly on the part.

faq.q: Why does the zone not show?
faq.a: It sits below the zone that owns the accent. Drag it up.

faq.q: Can Chat do this?
faq.a: Yes: name the part and the look, then check the preview.

faq.q: Why sample instead of naming the colour?
faq.a: Naming gives a nearby colour; sampling gives the exact one.

mistakes.symptom: The rear stays the old colour
mistakes.cause: The zone is below another
mistakes.fix: Move it to the top.

mistakes.symptom: The accent colour does not match the front
mistakes.cause: The colour was guessed
mistakes.fix: Use PICK COLOR FROM CAR.

protips: If there is a front accent to match, always sample it. It saves a lot of trial and error.

articles.title: Give the numbers, sponsors or stripes their own finish
articles.summary: To change number or sponsor material, isolate the intended artwork first. Use a checked layer restriction when available; on a flat paint use a checked local selection or mask. A colour pick alone may include the same colour elsewhere.
articles.what: Paint colour and spec response need separate decisions. A layer restriction uses visible layer ownership, not its name. Inspect what the layer actually contains, including other artwork sharing it. A flattened paint has no separate number or sponsor layer to select: colour matching can include repeated colours outside the intended element, and tolerance cannot distinguish two identical colours. Use source paint for an ordinary primary-base material change when preserving its paint is intended; it does not preserve that element's material response or disable other paint contributors.
when: You want the numbers gold chrome, the sponsors satin, or the stripes candy.
You want sponsors to look like vinyl rather than shiny paint.
how: Inspect whether the intended numbers or sponsors have their own visible artwork layer. Check its contents rather than trusting a label.
For suitable separate artwork, use MAKE ZONE on its layer card or select a zone and tick the actual layer under RESTRICT TO LAYERS. Check that the zone covers the intended visible artwork.

If the artwork shares a layer or the paint is flat, create a checked local selection or mask, or separate the artwork first. A colour pick is only a candidate selection; inspect every area it includes.
Choose the intended material in BASE. Use BASE COLOR Use source paint (spec only) if retaining the artwork is intended, and inspect other paint contributors separately.
Check the composed spec and intended target. Protect body material separately when only numbers or sponsors should change. Judge final appearance in the actual intended viewing conditions.

controls.label: Create a zone restricted to this layer
controls.effect: One click makes a zone that only covers that layer.

controls.label: RESTRICT TO LAYERS
controls.effect: Limits a zone to the ticked layers.

tips: Decide which element should change material and which should keep its existing material.
Check layer visibility and the selected layer IDs if a restricted zone covers nothing.
pitfalls: A layer called Numbers may contain other artwork.
Changing only spec can still change perceived colour under reflections.
A hidden or missing restricted layer does not become an unrestricted body target.

deep.heading: Flat artwork and repeated colours
deep.body: A flat TGA contains pixels, not semantic sponsor/number layers. Tightening colour tolerance does not separate identical colours in different places. A spatial selection or mask is needed to distinguish the intended element.

deep.heading: Visible ownership
deep.body: The inspected source-layer mask uses source alpha at least 128 and above-art alpha below 128. Opacity, clipping, visible effects and group visibility participate through the stack compositor; this is a binary ownership mask, not a promise of perfect visual edges.

faq.q: Can Chat change numbers?
faq.a: It can propose supported changes when the target is identifiable. A name alone does not prove separate number artwork. Inspect the actual target and proposed change before applying it.

faq.q: What tolerance on a flat paint?
faq.a: There is no universal safe tolerance. Colour matching may include the same colour elsewhere, even at zero tolerance. Use a checked local selection or mask for numbers or sponsors that share colours with the body.

faq.q: Does it also do sponsors and stripes?
faq.a: The same targeting principles apply: inspect actual layer contents and visible ownership, or use a checked local mask on flat/shared artwork. Source paint retains the reviewed primary paint pass, not the element's shine.

mistakes.symptom: The same colour changed outside the numbers
mistakes.cause: Colour selection also reached matching body or sponsor pixels
mistakes.fix: Use a checked local region/mask or genuinely separate artwork. Lower tolerance alone cannot separate identical colours.

articles.title: Make it pop
articles.summary: Find the biggest flat area and the strongest pair of colours. Push one to a deep glossy candy or pearl of its own colour, keep the other matte, satin or chrome, and add a faint flake.
articles.what: A livery pops when neighbouring areas differ in both colour and shine, not when everything gets more saturated. One glossy deep area beside a flat area reads as depth on the car, and a light flake across the body adds sparkle in the sun.
when: The car looks flat or samey.
You want one clear change that lifts the whole design.
how: Find the biggest area and the two colours that contrast most.
Give one of them a deep, glossy candy or pearl of its own colour with BASE COLOR set to use your paint.
Keep the other area matte or satin, or give it a chrome trim.
Add a subtle flake overlay on the body with + ADD SPEC OVERLAY, Strength 30 to 50.
Compare with the SOURCE view and stop when it reads clearly at arm's length.

controls.label: + ADD SPEC OVERLAY
controls.effect: A faint flake adds sparkle without changing the colour.

tips: Opposite colour and opposite shine beside each other is the strongest contrast.
Change one thing at a time so you can undo it cleanly.
pitfalls: Too many glossy areas cancel each other out. Keep one hero area.

deep.heading: Contrast of colour and shine
deep.body: A livery pops when neighbouring areas differ in both colour and shine, not when everything gets more saturated. One glossy deep area beside a flat area reads as depth on the car.

deep.heading: The recipe
deep.body: Find the biggest area and the two colours that contrast most. Give one a deep glossy candy or pearl of its own colour (BASE COLOR set to use your paint). Keep the other matte or satin, or give it a chrome trim. Add a subtle flake overlay on the body with Strength 30 to 50.

deep.heading: Stop early
deep.body: Compare with the SOURCE view and stop when it reads clearly at arm's length. Too many glossy areas cancel each other out: keep one hero area.

settings.Overlay: Flake on the body, Strength 30 to 50

faq.q: Should I boost saturation?
faq.a: No. Contrast in colour and shine matters more.

faq.q: How much flake?
faq.a: Subtle: Strength 30 to 50.

faq.q: How many glossy areas?
faq.a: One hero area.

mistakes.symptom: Everything looks the same
mistakes.cause: All areas glossy
mistakes.fix: Make the neighbour matte or satin.

mistakes.symptom: Hard to undo
mistakes.cause: Several changes at once
mistakes.fix: Change one thing at a time.

protips: View it small (zoomed out). If it still reads, it will read on track.

articles.title: Undo, go back and start over
articles.summary: Ctrl+Z takes back the last step, and every helper change has its own Undo button. To start the whole look over use Reset All Zones, or the Undo History panel to jump back several steps.
articles.what: There are three levels. One step back: Ctrl+Z or the Undo button under a helper answer. Several steps: press Undo more than once, with the Undo History list of recent actions to see where you are. A clean slate: Reset All Zones, which returns the list to the default five zones. The helper cannot delete zones itself; it mutes them and tells you where to delete.
when: The last change was wrong.
You want the base file back and clear zones.
how: Press Ctrl+Z, or press Undo under the helper's answer, to take back one step.
Open Undo History to see the list of recent actions.
To begin again, press Reset All Zones in the zones list.
Never mute every zone: a render needs at least one zone.
Save a project first if you might want the current look back.

controls.label: Undo
controls.effect: Takes back the last step.

controls.label: Reset All Zones
controls.effect: Back to the default five zones.

tips: Undo History lists your recent actions.
pitfalls: Undoing many steps after you reset by hand can bring back an old state. When you want the base file, reset instead.

deep.heading: Three levels
deep.body: One step back: Ctrl+Z or the Undo button under a helper answer. Several steps: press Undo more than once, with the Undo History list of recent actions to see where you are. A clean slate: Reset All Zones, which returns the list to the default five zones.

deep.body: The helper cannot delete zones itself; it mutes them and tells you where to delete. Never mute every zone: a render needs at least one zone.

deep.heading: Caution

articles.title: Change the whole car and keep the numbers and sponsors
articles.summary: Pattern Blend is not an exact sponsor-RGB guarantee: it retains hue/saturation while changing brightness. To protect numbers and sponsors, inspect actual layer content and exclude their coverage from unintended paint treatments. If artwork shares a raster, use a checked mask or separate it; layer names alone do not guarantee preservation. The per-Zone material-source blend itself has no paint RGB argument; other Base paint, patterns or later treatments can still change artwork, so that local helper fact is not a whole-render colour guarantee.
articles.what: A layer restriction limits the zone to the selected layer artwork. It protects numbers and sponsors only when they are outside that artwork and the selected coverage. Inspect the layer contribution rather than relying on names such as Car Paint or Body. If body paint and decals share a raster, use a checked mask or selection to exclude decals, or separate them before editing. Check the preview and rendered result against the original.
when: You want a new body colour or finish with the decals unchanged.
A previous whole-car look wiped the numbers.
how: Use the Layers eyes to inspect which artwork contains the body, numbers and sponsors. Names alone are not proof of their contents.
Restrict the body Zone to the verified body layer or checked region, excluding the number/sponsor pixels. If they share a layer or colour, separate the artwork or use a checked spatial mask.

For an ordinary primary material-only change choose Use source paint. Review other bases, paint patterns and colour/HSB adjustments separately; Pattern Blend can change brightness and is not exact RGB protection.
Compare the affected artwork with the original and use the relevant Undo if protected pixels changed. Inspect the actual output and number mode before accepting it.

controls.label: RESTRICT TO LAYERS
controls.effect: Limits a zone to the ticked layers.

tips: Inspect a layer with its eye before selecting it; its name alone does not prove which pixels belong to it.
An unrestricted zone can affect numbers and logos within its coverage. Check the actual preview and rendered paint.
pitfalls: A layer may contain both body paint and protected artwork. A layer restriction alone cannot separate those pixels.
A flat paint may have body paint and numbers of the same colour; colour picking can select both.
aliases: recolour the car keep the numbers
whole car new colour keep sponsors

deep.heading: Check the body artwork first
deep.body: A layer restriction limits the zone to the selected layer artwork. It protects numbers and sponsors only when they are outside that artwork and the selected coverage. Inspect the layer contribution rather than relying on names such as Car Paint or Body. If body paint and decals share a raster, use a checked mask or selection to exclude decals, or separate them before editing. Check the preview and rendered result against the original.

deep.heading: Set and verify the scope
deep.body: Inspect the actual body artwork layer. Restrict the zone to that artwork only if it excludes the numbers and sponsors. For mixed artwork, use a checked mask or separate layers. Apply the colour or finish and compare the preview and rendered paint with the original; use Undo if the protected artwork changes.

deep.heading: Chat and flat paints
deep.body: Tell the helper which artwork to change and which numbers or sponsors to preserve. Check its proposed scope and actual preview; a reply saying it kept them is not proof. If the scope cannot isolate the artwork, use a checked mask or separate layers first. Use Undo for an unwanted change. A flat TGA has no layer separation. Colour picking or a box can include numbers and logos, including artwork that shares the body colour. Inspect the selected coverage and exclude protected artwork before applying a finish. A box or colour name does not identify UV panels or prove preservation. Undo a result that alters artwork you meant to keep.

examples.result: If the selected layer is isolated body artwork and the zone coverage excludes the protected decals, this setup limits the finish to that artwork. Verify the preview and rendered result.

examples.goal: Illustrative setup after checking that the named body layer contains only the intended body artwork.

faq.q: Why did my numbers vanish?
faq.a: Inspect what the zone reached. It may have lacked a layer limit, or the selected artwork layer may also contain the numbers. Undo the unwanted change and isolate the intended body artwork before trying again.

faq.q: Can I include the numbers on purpose?
faq.a: Yes, explicitly include the verified number artwork in the scope and check the preview. A number layer name alone is not enough.

faq.q: What if there are no layers?
faq.a: A flat TGA has no layer separation. Colour picking or a box can include numbers and logos, including artwork that shares the body colour. Inspect the selected coverage and exclude protected artwork before applying a finish. A box or colour name does not identify UV panels or prove preservation. Undo a result that alters artwork you meant to keep.

faq.q: Is every Foundation option safe for shine without recolouring sponsor artwork?
faq.a: No whole-shelf guarantee. Twenty plain Foundation materials can retain source paint with Use source paint (spec only), but five gem/shift members have colour-bearing paint functions. Source-colour preservation does not automatically protect sponsor material. Check actual layer contents and zone targeting; a material change still changes the lit appearance.

faq.q: My sponsor is still there but looks shiny. Should I repaint it?
faq.a: Check the material map and target coverage before repainting. Retained colour pixels can look different after metal/roughness/clearcoat or alpha changes. Inspect those channels and the sponsor footprint, then correct the intended material contribution; appearance alone does not prove the paint was recoloured.

mistakes.symptom: Numbers covered
mistakes.cause: The zone coverage included the numbers, possibly on the same layer or in a same-colour selection.
mistakes.fix: Undo, inspect the selected coverage and exclude the number artwork before applying the change.

mistakes.symptom: Sponsors changed
mistakes.cause: The selected scope reached the sponsor artwork. A body layer restriction can still include sponsors on that layer.
mistakes.fix: Undo the change, inspect the layer contribution and use isolated artwork or a checked exclusion mask.

protips: Always look at the numbers in the CAR view after a body-wide change. It takes five seconds.

deep.heading: Current source-qualified workflow
deep.body:
The top-bar Customer ID is an account identifier used for output filenames, not the race-number artwork. SPB accepts number text through Text (T) or Car > Number Kit. 2. For editable number text, use Text (T) or Car > Number Kit. Select the intended existing kit to edit its number/style, or create a new kit deliberately. A raster number already baked into a flat image is not automatically converted into editable text.
3. Number Kit previews changes as temporary layers. Inspect its Existing numbers Replace Existing/Add Alongside choice and actual locations. Check the exact template, free-placement fallback and Turn Each Place; automatic turns are not a verified UV calibration.
4. Use Add Number Kit to commit, or Cancel/Esc to abandon that session. If old numbers are baked into the source, replacing kit layers does not erase those source pixels; work from a clean source or edit the intended artwork separately.

faq.q: How do I put a number on my car?
faq.a: Choose Sim-Stamped Number to let iRacing stamp it, or add your own number picture with Actions > Place image... in the layer list and choose Custom Number.

faq.q: Where do I type my car number?
faq.a: Use Text (T) or the Number field in Car > Number Kit for painted artwork. The top-bar Customer ID is your account ID for filenames, not that number.

faq.q: Can I change the colour of the numbers on my template?
faq.a: Yes. Press the zone icon on the Numbers layer and set BASE COLOR to Use solid color, or give it a finish.

faq.q: Why do I see two numbers?
faq.a: Check separate causes: old numbers baked into the source, Add Alongside versus Replace Existing kit layers, or an iRacing stamp over custom number artwork. A number-mode toggle does not remove old raster pixels.

faq.q: How do I change just the car number for each driver?
faq.a: For one paint, edit its number text or existing Number Kit and inspect every intended placement. For a roster on the same car, use Car > League Pack with separate Customer ID and Number columns; leave optional artwork changes empty and verify its preview/status.

faq.q: How do I put the big number on the roof?
faq.a: Make the number as a transparent PNG (or use your PSD's Numbers layer), choose Actions > Place image..., then Move (V) it onto the roof panel on the flat sheet and size it with Transform (Ctrl+T). The roof sits across the middle of a typical stock-car sheet; the Wire layer shows the outlines. The Text tool (press T) has a Font menu in the tool options bar, or you can choose the font when you make the PNG. Choose Custom Number and match Hide Car Numbers in iRacing.

faq.q: Our car carries its number on the roof, how do I place a large number there?
faq.a: Make the number as a transparent PNG, open the layer list and choose Actions > Place image..., then place it with Move (V) and size it with Transform (Ctrl+T) onto the roof panel. Choose Custom Number so it is your art.

faq.q: Why is my race number mirrored or flipped on one side?
faq.a: Inspect Number Kit’s Turn Each Place and the exact template. Missing direction data can be assumed; manual turn options and free placement do not prove physical panel mapping.

faq.q: My race number is mirrored or flipped on one side
faq.a: Inspect Number Kit’s Turn Each Place and the exact template. Missing direction data can be assumed; manual turn options and free placement do not prove physical panel mapping.

faq.q: Every driver has their own number, how do we change only the number without redoing the paint?
faq.a: Car > League Pack accepts a driver roster on one exact template. Customer ID names each output; Number is the artwork. Keep optional colour/sponsor/name changes empty and inspect each preview and result. This does not certify cross-car mapping or every native batch output.

faq.q: The race number on the passenger side is flipped
faq.a: The two sides of the sheet are not placed the same way up, so a mirrored number flips: use FLIP or ROT 90 on the layer card, or place the number separately on that side with its own zone (mirror recipe caveat).

mistakes.symptom: No number at all in iRacing
mistakes.cause: Custom Number is chosen but the paint has no number art.
mistakes.fix: Add a number layer, or choose Sim-Stamped Number and set Hide Car Numbers OFF.

mistakes.symptom: iRacing shows paint-shop colours, not my paint
mistakes.cause: The Shokker box and iRacing's Hide Car Numbers disagree, so iRacing finds no file.
mistakes.fix: Make them agree (Custom = ON, Sim-Stamped = OFF), restart iRacing if you changed it, render, Ctrl+R.

protips: Not sure which file iRacing wants? Render once in each mode: both files stay in the folder and iRacing picks the one it needs.

articles.title: Glow-in-the-dark and light-up paint: what is possible
articles.summary: A neon-looking palette or Outer Glow halo is painted colour, not proof of self-lit emission. The reviewed Jukebox Neon generator supplies RGB and metal/roughness/clearcoat fields, with no emission field. Choose Use source paint for ordinary primary material-only work; appearance still needs simulator checks.
articles.what: Separate the requested look from the data the app writes. Jukebox Neon’s current registered builder has curved coloured rails and spatial material fields, not an emission output. Layer Outer Glow draws a blurred coloured halo around the source layer with Canvas2D, then composites it into the picture; it does not create a lamp or emissive shader. Colour contrast can suggest neon, but its usefulness and readability are visual choices to assess in actual lighting. The official iRacing Paint Textures article, modified December2019, describes spec alpha as masking reflections/specular lighting. It does not document alpha as a light source, and its old blue-unused statement was superseded by later clearcoat support. Do not promise that alpha0 removes every lighting component on every current car.
when: You want a neon-looking colour design, a halo around artwork, or clarification about emission and spec alpha.
how: Identify the intended target: body area, an existing number/logo layer, or material texture over existing artwork.
For a coloured neon design, inspect the exact finish and own-colour palette before using it. A name alone is not a verified recommendation.
For the reviewed Jukebox Neon primary material pass over existing paint, choose Use source paint and check other contributors and target masks separately.
For a halo around a separate artwork layer, inspect that layer’s Outer Glow settings and preview the result; merged artwork requires isolation first.
Check readable detail in the simulator in representative daylight and night conditions. Neither a palette nor a preview proves self-lighting.
tips: Keep the bright parts small; a whole car in neon green looks pastel, not glowing.
Outer Glow size runs from 1 to 50 and opacity from 0 to 100; a small size reads as a crisp neon edge.
pitfalls: Setting the lighting mask (alpha) to 0 does not make a spot glow: it removes the lighting response, so the spot looks flat.
Glow finishes bring their own colours; switching BASE COLOR to a solid colour can lose the glowing contrast.
aliases: make my car glow at night

deep.heading: Painted halo versus emission
deep.body: The current Outer Glow path uses shadow colour/blur and repeated Canvas2D drawImage calls, removes the original layer shape from the halo canvas, and composites the halo into the picture. The reviewed Jukebox generator outputs RGB and M/R/C only. These source facts establish painted and material effects, not a global proof about every simulator shader.

deep.heading: Alpha is a mask, not a glow control
deep.body: The2019 official documentation describes masking reflection/specular effects with spec alpha, not emission. Current JS/server code carries a clamped override to the zone helper and car spec writer. Ten synthetic helper/writer cases preserve RGBA bytes on export, but full live rendering and current simulator appearance remain separate acceptance checks. Low alpha is not a documented emission workflow.

faq.q: Can I make a glow-in-the-dark paint?
faq.a: A neon-looking palette or Outer Glow halo is painted colour, not proof of self-lit emission. The reviewed Jukebox Neon generator supplies RGB and metal/roughness/clearcoat fields, with no emission field. Choose Use source paint for ordinary primary material-only work; appearance still needs simulator checks.

faq.q: Does setting the alpha or lighting mask to zero make it glow?
faq.a: The official2019 iRacing guide describes spec alpha as a reflection/specular mask, not an emission source. Do not use alpha0 as a glow recipe or assume it removes every lighting component on every current car.

faq.q: Which finishes look like they glow?
faq.a: Search for the intended design concept, then inspect the exact active finish. Jukebox Neon has source-reviewed curved RGB rails and material fields; its name does not supply emission or verify suitability. Other glow-named catalog examples have not been accepted as recommendations in this audit.

faq.q: How do I make the car glow like neon?
faq.a: Use a deliberate coloured design or a painted halo, then inspect daylight/night readability in the simulator. Outer Glow composites a halo into the image; Jukebox Neon outputs RGB/material fields. Neither establishes self-lit emission.

faq.q: Does Jukebox Neon generate a self-lit emission channel?
faq.a: Its reviewed current builder returns RGB paint and metal/roughness/clearcoat, with no emission field. Neon describes the design concept. A glowing-looking palette does not prove a car can emit light.

faq.q: Can I keep my original colours while using the neon material map?
faq.a: For the reviewed Jukebox Neon primary base, Use source paint skips its authored paint palette while its material map can remain. Check target masks and other contributors separately. Do not choose the finish’s own colour when you intend to keep source artwork, and do not assume a neon name supplies an emission field. faq.q: Are all glow-named finishes guaranteed to look good at night?
